topic.name: Cryptographic hash function
topic.definition: A deterministic algorithm that maps an arbitrary-length binary input to a fixed-length digest, with security goals including preimage resistance, second-preimage resistance, and collision resistance.

source_scope.primary_source: User-supplied Wikipedia article text: Cryptographic hash function
source_scope.scope_note: The graph follows the supplied article's terminology and coverage, while adding explicit relationship structure, schema, patterns, and cautious engineering rules for machine use.
source_derived_content: Merkle–Damgård, wide-pipe, sponge, and HAIFA constructions
source_scope.editorial_caveat: Algorithm status and parameter recommendations change. Use current standards and expert review for production decisions; the graph is not a substitute for a cryptographic design review.

entities.name: Cryptographic hash function
entities.description: A deterministic algorithm mapping an arbitrary-length binary message to a fixed-length digest, designed to provide cryptographic security properties.

entities.name: Hash function
entities.description: A function that maps input values to hash outputs; not every hash function is cryptographically secure.

entities.name: Message / input
entities.description: The arbitrary-length binary string supplied to a hash algorithm.

entities.name: Hash digest
entities.description: The fixed-length output produced by hashing a message; also called a message digest, hash value, or digital fingerprint.

entities.name: Fixed-length output
entities.description: The digest length is defined by the algorithm or selected output mode, regardless of ordinary input length.

entities.name: Determinism
entities.description: The same input and algorithm parameters produce the same digest.

entities.name: Avalanche effect
entities.description: A small input change should cause a large, unpredictable change in the output bits.

entities.name: Preimage resistance
entities.description: Given a target digest h, it should be computationally infeasible to find any m for which H(m)=h.

entities.name: Second-preimage resistance
entities.description: Given m1, it should be infeasible to find a different m2 with H(m1)=H(m2).

entities.name: Collision resistance
entities.description: It should be infeasible to find any two distinct messages m1 and m2 with equal digests.

entities.name: Birthday bound
entities.description: For an ideal n-bit digest, generic collision search costs roughly 2^(n/2), while generic preimage search costs roughly 2^n.

entities.name: Random oracle model
entities.description: An idealized model treating a hash as a deterministic function whose outputs appear random for distinct new inputs.

entities.name: Length-extension attack
entities.description: For certain Merkle–Damgård hashes, an attacker knowing H(m) and len(m) may calculate H(m || padding || m′) without knowing m.

entities.name: Hash collision
entities.description: A pair of different messages that produce the same digest under the same hash algorithm and parameters.

entities.name: Cryptanalysis
entities.description: The study of weaknesses and attacks against cryptographic algorithms and protocols.

entities.name: Cryptographic agility
entities.description: The ability to change algorithms, digest sizes, and parameters as security recommendations evolve.

entities.name: Checksum
entities.description: A general error-detection value; ordinary checksums are not necessarily resistant to intentional manipulation.

entities.name: CRC-32
entities.description: A cyclic redundancy check useful for accidental-error detection but not a cryptographic hash.

entities.name: Integrity verification
entities.description: Comparing a freshly computed digest with a trusted expected digest to detect data changes.

entities.name: Chain of trust
entities.description: The trust path by which a digest or signature is obtained from an authenticated source.

entities.name: Content-addressable storage (CAS)
entities.description: Storage in which content is retrieved using a digest-derived content address rather than a name or physical location.

entities.name: Content address
entities.description: A digest-derived identifier used to locate or identify content.

entities.name: Content deduplication
entities.description: Detecting identical content using content-derived identifiers, subject to the system's collision-handling assumptions.

entities.name: Hash table
entities.description: A data structure that uses hash outputs to choose storage buckets; non-cryptographic hashes may be vulnerable to deliberate collision attacks.

entities.name: Digital signature
entities.description: A signing scheme commonly hashes a message before signing a fixed-size digest; signature verification alone still depends on the full scheme and key trust.

entities.name: Message authentication code (MAC)
entities.description: A keyed integrity/authentication tag that allows parties sharing a secret key to verify message authenticity and integrity.

entities.name: HMAC
entities.description: A keyed message authentication construction built from a cryptographic hash function, designed to avoid pitfalls of naive hash-based authentication.

entities.name: Password hashing
entities.description: Transforming a password into a stored verifier; general-purpose fast hashes are unsuitable alone for modern password storage.

entities.name: Password salt
entities.description: A random, non-secret value included in password derivation so identical passwords do not share the same stored result and precomputed tables are less useful.

entities.name: Key derivation function (KDF)
entities.description: A function that derives keys or password verifiers; password KDFs are configured to impose computational and sometimes memory cost.

entities.name: Key stretching
entities.description: Increasing the cost of password guessing through repeated work and/or memory requirements.

entities.name: Proof of work
entities.description: A protocol technique requiring a requester to find a value satisfying a hash-based condition, while verification remains cheap.

entities.name: Hashcash
entities.description: A proof-of-work system that requires a hash meeting a leading-zero-bit target, originally used as an anti-abuse token.

entities.name: Bitcoin mining
entities.description: A proof-of-work process that searches for block headers meeting a network-defined hash target.

entities.name: File fingerprint
entities.description: A digest used as a compact identifier for file or object content.

entities.name: Peer-to-peer file sharing
entities.description: Systems that use content hashes or hash trees to identify and verify shared data.

entities.name: Magnet link
entities.description: A link that identifies peer-to-peer content using a content hash or related identifier rather than requiring a direct file URL.

entities.name: Hash tree
entities.description: A tree of hashes that can support efficient verification of data subsets and identify a root digest for a larger object.

entities.name: Merkle tree
entities.description: A hash tree in which parent nodes are derived from child hashes and a root commits to the tree's content.

entities.name: Commitment scheme
entities.description: A protocol allowing a party to commit to a value while keeping it hidden until later revelation; a digest can serve as a simple commitment in appropriate contexts.

entities.name: Block cipher
entities.description: A keyed fixed-block encryption primitive; specialized constructions can use block-cipher-like components to build hashes.

entities.name: Compression function
entities.description: A fixed-input-size function that combines a chaining state and a message block into a smaller or fixed-size state.

entities.name: Merkle–Damgård construction
entities.description: An iterative hash construction processing padded message blocks through a compression function; many classical hashes use this structure.

entities.name: Wide-pipe design
entities.description: A design with an internal state wider than the final digest, intended to mitigate some structural attacks.

entities.name: Narrow-pipe design
entities.description: A design where internal state width closely matches output width, associated with several structural limitations in straightforward Merkle–Damgård applications.

entities.name: Sponge construction
entities.description: A construction that absorbs input into an internal state and squeezes output; used by Keccak/SHA-3 and extendable-output functions.

entities.name: HAIFA construction
entities.description: A hash construction framework adding features such as counters and salts to an iterative design.

entities.name: Davies–Meyer construction
entities.description: A compression-function construction often used with block-cipher-like components in hash designs.

entities.name: Digest truncation
entities.description: Returning fewer bits than an underlying hash state or longer digest; security depends on construction and selected output length.

entities.name: Concatenation of hash outputs
entities.description: Combining digests from multiple algorithms; security depends on the combiner and assumptions about component algorithms.

entities.name: Pseudorandom number generator (PRNG)
entities.description: A generator that expands a seed into a sequence intended to appear pseudorandom; hashes can be used with a secret seed and counter.

entities.name: Stream cipher
entities.description: An encryption primitive that combines a keystream with plaintext; hash-based constructions may help generate pseudorandom streams.

entities.name: Non-cryptographic hash function
entities.description: A hash designed for speed or distribution rather than resistance to adversarial attacks.

entities.name: Password brute-force attack
entities.description: Trying candidate passwords and comparing derived verifiers; fast general-purpose hashes enable high guess rates.

entities.name: Rainbow table
entities.description: A precomputed time-memory tradeoff table for reversing password hash values over a candidate space; salts reduce reuse of such tables.

entities.name: Denial-of-service attack
entities.description: An attack intended to exhaust or disrupt a service; predictable hash-table collisions can be used to increase processing cost.

entities.name: Randomized hashing
entities.description: A technique used in some signature and hashing contexts to reduce risks from adversarially crafted messages or collisions.

entities.name: MD4
entities.description: Older 128-bit digest design; historically influential but cryptographically broken.

entities.name: MD5
entities.description: Produces a 128-bit (16-byte) digest. Practical collisions are known; unsuitable for security-sensitive collision-resistant uses.

entities.name: SHA-0
entities.description: Original Secure Hash Standard algorithm published in 1993 and withdrawn/replaced shortly thereafter.

entities.name: SHA-1
entities.description: Produces a 160-bit (20-byte) digest. Practical collision attacks exist; do not use for new collision-resistant security applications.

entities.name: RIPEMD-160
entities.description: Produces a 160-bit (20-byte) digest; the supplied article describes it as not broken at the time of its text, but algorithm choice should follow current standards guidance.

entities.name: Whirlpool
entities.description: Produces a 512-bit (64-byte) digest and is based on a substantially modified AES-like design.

entities.name: SHA-2
entities.description: Family including SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256.

entities.name: SHA-224
entities.description: SHA-2 variant with a 224-bit (28-byte) output.

entities.name: SHA-256
entities.description: SHA-2 algorithm with a 256-bit (32-byte) output; Merkle–Damgård-family and susceptible to length extension when used naively.

entities.name: SHA-384
entities.description: SHA-2 variant with a 384-bit (48-byte) output.

entities.name: SHA-512
entities.description: SHA-2 algorithm with a 512-bit (64-byte) output; commonly efficient on 64-bit systems.

entities.name: SHA-512/224
entities.description: SHA-512-derived variant with a 224-bit output.

entities.name: SHA-512/256
entities.description: SHA-512-derived variant with a 256-bit output; output truncation changes relevant structural properties.

entities.name: SHA-3
entities.description: NIST-standardized family based on Keccak and the sponge construction; provides 224-, 256-, 384-, and 512-bit outputs.

entities.name: Keccak
entities.description: Sponge-based cryptographic primitive family designed by Guido Bertoni, Joan Daemen, Michael Peeters, and Gilles Van Assche; SHA-3 is based on it.

entities.name: SHAKE-128
entities.description: SHAKE function with configurable output length; the 128 designation indicates security strength, not a fixed output size.

entities.name: SHAKE-256
entities.description: SHAKE function with configurable output length; the 256 designation indicates security strength, not a fixed output size.

entities.name: BLAKE
entities.description: SHA-3 competition finalist family with configurable digest sizes.

entities.name: BLAKE2
entities.description: Efficient hash family designed in part as a replacement for broken MD5/SHA-1 use cases; BLAKE2b is optimized for 64-bit platforms.

entities.name: BLAKE2b
entities.description: BLAKE2 variant optimized for 64-bit platforms and known for high software performance.

entities.name: BLAKE2s
entities.description: BLAKE2 variant oriented toward smaller architectures; BLAKE3's compression function is closely based on it.

entities.name: BLAKE3
entities.description: Single hash algorithm announced in 2020, using a Merkle-tree internal design and supporting high parallelism; its compression design is based on BLAKE2s with seven rounds.

entities.name: Skein
entities.description: SHA-3 competition finalist with configurable output and a construction that can produce arbitrary-length output.

entities.name: SWIFFT
entities.description: A function with provable collision-resistance properties under stated ideal-lattice assumptions, but its linearity means it does not provide all desirable random-like hash properties.

entities.name: SM3
entities.description: Cryptographic hash algorithm primarily standardized/used in China.

entities.name: Streebog / GOST R 34.11-2012
entities.description: Russian cryptographic hash standard.

entities.name: GOST R 34.11-94
entities.description: Older Soviet/Russian hash algorithm; deprecated in the supplied article's description.

entities.name: LSH hash
entities.description: Hash family associated with South Korea.

entities.name: Kupyna
entities.description: Ukrainian cryptographic hash algorithm.

entities.name: SHAttered collision demonstration
entities.description: Practical collision demonstration against SHA-1 announced by Google in 2017.

entities.name: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
entities.description: General-purpose block cipher; can be repurposed in hash constructions but design goals and security considerations differ from purpose-built hash components.

entities.name: Argon2
entities.description: Password hashing/key derivation function designed to impose configurable memory and computational costs.

entities.name: scrypt
entities.description: Memory-hard password-based key derivation function.

entities.name: PBKDF2
entities.description: Password-based key derivation function that uses repeated pseudorandom-function iterations.

entities.name: bcrypt
entities.description: Password hashing function designed to make password guessing more expensive.

entities.name: Balloon hashing
entities.description: Password hashing/KDF approach using repeated work and memory to slow offline guessing.

entities.name: Transport Layer Security (TLS)
entities.description: Protocol whose signatures, certificates, and integrity mechanisms use cryptographic primitives; the supplied article discusses historic concatenated MD5/SHA-1 use in older TLS/SSL versions.

entities.name: Git object hashing
entities.description: Version control system that uses content hashes to identify objects; historical object formats used SHA-1.

entities.name: Mercurial object hashing
entities.description: Version control system that uses hashes to identify repository content and history objects.

entities.name: Monotone
entities.description: Source control system cited as using hashes for content, trees, and ancestry information.

entities.name: eD2k hash/link
entities.description: Peer-to-peer file identification using an MD4-variant hash combined with file size.

entities.name: National Security Agency (NSA)
entities.description: U.S. agency credited in the supplied article with designing SHA-2 and associated with the Secure Hash Algorithm lineage.

entities.name: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
entities.description: U.S. standards agency that published Secure Hash Standards and selected SHA-3.

entities.name: Guido Bertoni
entities.description: One of the designers of Keccak.

entities.name: Joan Daemen
entities.description: One of the designers of Keccak.

entities.name: Michael Peeters
entities.description: One of the designers of Keccak.

entities.name: Gilles Van Assche
entities.description: One of the designers of Keccak.

entities.name: Ronald Rivest
entities.description: Designed MD5 in 1991 as a successor to MD4.

entities.name: Jean-Philippe Aumasson
entities.description: Co-creator of BLAKE2 and BLAKE3.

entities.name: Samuel Neves
entities.description: Co-creator of BLAKE2 and BLAKE3.

entities.name: Zooko Wilcox-O'Hearn
entities.description: Co-creator of BLAKE2 and BLAKE3.

entities.name: Christian Winnerlein
entities.description: Co-creator of BLAKE2.

entities.name: Birthday attack
entities.description: Generic collision-search strategy exploiting birthday probabilities; for n-bit ideal hashes, collision work is on the order of 2^(n/2).

entities.name: Preimage attack
entities.description: Attack attempting to find any input matching a specified digest.

entities.name: Second-preimage attack
entities.description: Attack attempting to find a distinct input matching the digest of a given message.

entities.name: Chosen-prefix collision
entities.description: A collision technique that aims to create two messages with attacker-chosen prefixes and matching hash results; practical consequences depend on the algorithm.

entities.name: SHAttered attack
entities.description: The 2017 practical SHA-1 collision demonstration, showing SHA-1 is unsuitable for collision-sensitive security uses.

entities.name: MD5 certificate collision attack
entities.description: A practical 2008 attack used MD5 collisions to undermine certificate trust.

entities.name: Hash-table collision denial of service
entities.description: An attacker supplies inputs that concentrate into the same hash-table buckets, causing excessive work when the table hash is not adversarially robust.

entities.name: Secret random seed
entities.description: A seed used with a counter and hash-based construction to derive pseudorandom output.

entities.name: Counter
entities.description: A changing value combined with a seed in hash-based PRNG constructions.

entities.name: Password verifier database
entities.description: Stores salts and derived password verifiers rather than plaintext passwords.

entities.name: Trusted publisher
entities.description: The authenticated source from which a file and its expected digest are obtained.

entities.name: Downloaded file
entities.description: A file whose computed digest can be compared against a trusted expected digest.

entities.name: Merkle root
entities.description: The root digest that commits to the leaves and structure of a Merkle tree.

entities.name: Hash-based PRNG construction
entities.description: A generator construction combining a secret seed with a counter and applying a hash-based primitive.

entities.name: Naive hash-based authentication
entities.description: Authentication designs that directly hash a message with an appended secret can be vulnerable to length-extension attacks.

entities.name: Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP)
entities.description: Legacy wireless security protocol that used CRC for integrity; CRC's linearity made manipulation attacks possible.

entities.name: NIST SHA-3 competition
entities.description: NIST process that evaluated candidate hash functions and selected Keccak for SHA-3.

entities.name: Merkle–Damgård length padding
entities.description: Unambiguous padding, including message length, is crucial to the security of Merkle–Damgård iteration.

entities.name: Message block
entities.description: A fixed-size portion of a message processed by an iterative hash construction.

entities.name: Chaining state
entities.description: The evolving internal state passed between compression-function steps.

entities.name: Digest length
entities.description: Output length measured in bits or bytes; it affects generic preimage and collision security bounds.

entities.name: Security strength
entities.description: An estimate of attack work in bits; ideal n-bit hashes offer about n-bit generic preimage strength and n/2-bit collision strength.

entities.name: 16 KiB block
entities.description: A 16 KiB block size mentioned in the separate torrent-v2 topic; not a general cryptographic hash standard. Included only as a cross-domain context node.

architecture_patterns.name: Secure file verification
architecture_patterns.purpose: Detect modification or substitution of downloaded content.
steps: Obtain the expected digest from an authenticated/trusted source.
Compute the digest of the received file with a suitable modern algorithm.
Compare values using the correct algorithm and encoding.
If a mismatch occurs, reject or investigate the file; if it matches, interpret the result only within the trust model.
caveats: A digest posted beside a file on the same unauthenticated channel may be replaced together with the file.
A matching hash does not prove that software is benign or that the publisher is trustworthy.

architecture_patterns.name: Password storage with a password KDF
architecture_patterns.purpose: Reduce the rate of offline password guessing after a verifier database is exposed.
steps: Generate a unique random salt per password.
Derive a verifier using a password KDF such as Argon2, scrypt, bcrypt, or PBKDF2 with appropriate parameters.
Store the algorithm identifier, parameters, salt, and verifier.
On login, recompute and compare; upgrade parameters as policy changes.
caveats: Do not use a fast hash such as raw SHA-256 or SHA-1 alone for password storage.
Parameter choices should follow current platform and standards guidance.

architecture_patterns.name: HMAC message authentication
architecture_patterns.purpose: Authenticate messages using a shared secret and a standardized keyed construction.
steps: Agree on a secure hash and shared secret key.
Compute the HMAC over the canonical message representation.
Transmit the message and authentication tag.
Receiver recomputes the HMAC and compares tags using an appropriate constant-time comparison.
caveats: Do not substitute naive hash(secret || message) constructions for HMAC.
Key management and message canonicalization remain important.

architecture_patterns.name: Content-addressed storage
architecture_patterns.purpose: Address and deduplicate objects based on content.
steps: Select a collision-resistant hash and a canonical byte representation.
Hash the content to derive a content address.
Store the object and index its address to physical storage.
On retrieval, recompute the hash to verify content integrity.
caveats: Collision handling and algorithm migration should be part of the design.
The content address is not automatically a claim of publisher authenticity.

architecture_patterns.name: Merkle-tree verification
architecture_patterns.purpose: Commit to a large data set and verify components using a root digest and authentication path.
steps: Hash each leaf using an unambiguous encoding.
Hash internal nodes from their child hashes.
Publish or authenticate the root digest.
Verify a selected leaf by recomputing its path to the root.
caveats: Tree layout, leaf/node domain separation, and encoding must be specified to avoid ambiguity.

architecture_patterns.name: Hash-based proof of work
architecture_patterns.purpose: Make request creation moderately costly while allowing cheap validation.
steps: Define a target predicate over a hash output.
Vary a nonce or candidate header and compute hashes until the predicate passes.
Send the candidate and proof.
Verifier performs one or a small number of hash computations and checks the predicate.
caveats: Difficulty must be calibrated; proof of work does not itself establish the truth or legitimacy of the submitted content.

architecture_patterns.name: Cryptographic hash algorithm migration
architecture_patterns.purpose: Retire weak digest algorithms while maintaining interoperability.
steps: Inventory every algorithm use and stored identifier format.
Choose a modern algorithm appropriate to the use case and threat model.
Version formats and APIs so algorithm identity is explicit.
Where feasible, verify old objects and add new digests; plan dual-read or staged migration.
Monitor standards and cryptanalysis and retire obsolete formats.
caveats: A digest's byte length alone does not uniquely identify the algorithm.
Do not assume legacy digests become secure because they are combined with a modern digest.

derived_rules.statement: A cryptographic hash is not encryption and has no decryption key or general inverse operation.
A matching digest proves only a content match relative to the expected digest and trust chain; it does not establish that the content is safe or benign.
For an ideal n-bit hash, generic preimage work is about 2^n and generic collision work about 2^(n/2); real algorithms may be weaker due to cryptanalysis.
Fast general-purpose hashes should not be used alone to store passwords; use a salted password KDF with current recommended parameters.
For hash-based message authentication, use HMAC or another reviewed construction rather than naive secret-prefix/suffix hashing.
MD5 and SHA-1 are unsuitable for new applications that depend on collision resistance.
CRC-32 and similar checksums detect accidental corruption but do not provide cryptographic protection against intentional manipulation.
Persist the algorithm name/version and output parameters alongside a digest; digest bytes alone are not a robust self-describing identifier.

examples.title: File digest comparison
examples.input: A downloaded archive and a trusted SHA-256 digest string.
steps: Compute SHA-256 over the exact downloaded bytes.
Encode the result consistently, commonly as hexadecimal.
Compare with the authenticated expected digest.
examples.output: Equal digests provide strong evidence of byte-for-byte identity under SHA-256's security assumptions and the trust model.

examples.title: Leading-zero proof of work
examples.input: A candidate message/header plus a nonce.
steps: Hash the candidate.
Check whether the digest begins with the required number of zero bits.
If not, vary the nonce and repeat.
examples.output: A valid candidate is relatively cheap to verify; expected search effort grows exponentially with the number of required leading zero bits.

examples.title: Digest commitment
examples.input: A secret solution m held by Alice.
steps: Alice computes H(m) and publishes the digest before revealing m.
Bob later computes H(m) over the revealed solution.
They compare the result to the earlier commitment.
examples.output: The matching digest supports the claim that the revealed solution matches the committed value, assuming the hash and protocol are appropriate.

examples.title: Salted password verifier
examples.input: Password candidate, unique random salt, KDF name and parameters.
steps: Derive a verifier with the selected password KDF.
Store the salt, algorithm parameters and verifier, not the plaintext password.
At login, derive again and compare.
examples.output: Unique salts reduce cross-account precomputation and KDF cost slows each password guess.
